title: Why the State Bank just raised interest rates
credits: Photos: Shujaat Muzaffar, Muhammad Amir / Unsplash · Map: Natural Earth
lines: The State Bank of Pakistan has raised its key interest rate for the first time since June.
The policy rate goes up by half a percentage point, to twelve percent.
Nine of the ten members of the Monetary Policy Committee voted for the rise.
The reason is inflation. Prices rose ten point three percent in September, well above the State Bank's target of five to seven percent.
The committee says the war in the Middle East and higher energy costs have worsened the inflation outlook.
It also pointed to problems with wheat supplies at home.
The State Bank says the rise is needed to keep inflation expectations anchored, and to stop the energy shock spreading to other prices.
It expects the economy to grow between three and a half and four and a half percent this fiscal year.
Foreign reserves at the State Bank are about twenty-one and a half billion dollars, around three months of imports.
Businesses are divided. Foreign investors back the move, but industry warns that dearer loans will hurt exports and growth.
For ordinary Pakistanis, higher rates mean costlier loans, but better returns on savings.
